summary:
Risaralda department operates under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presentation of a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

The counterweight is lethal violence, documented nationally rather than inside Risaralda. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon, no one had been arrested although police interrogated local residents, President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. Earlier fatal attacks recalled in the same reporting include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Guajira, flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals have been posted since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, campaign flyers circulated on streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate targets; trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, was given one week by three armed men to leave town or be killed and fled at night after hiding for a week. Discrimination there confines trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise. None of the reviewed sources documents a legal provision, enforcement action or incident specific to Risaralda.
tangentialFactors:
The armed-group threat documented in Caquetá is the pattern most likely to bleed across departmental lines, because the groups responsible operate in several parts of the country and the 2016 peace agreement did not dissolve them. Flyer campaigns naming trans people as military targets appeared in Guajira from March 2024 and in Caquetá in 2024, and the reporting frames the violence as calculated brutality persisting amid a decades-long civil conflict rather than as isolated crime. A visitor should not read Risaralda's absence from that reporting as an absence of the groups behind it.

Discrimination that shapes daily life is economic as much as physical: in Caquetá, trans women are described as having few options beyond hairdressing and sex work, and eight trans women were killed nationally between February and April 2024 against 41 in 2023. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case. Set against neighbouring jurisdictions, Colombia's statutory position — notary-based marker change, self-recognition without surgery, trans and non-binary document markers — is stronger than that of most Latin American states, which is precisely the gap the UN Independent Expert identified between institutional progress and lived experience.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on their cédula by signing a document before a notary, a procedure approved in June 2015; the earlier judicial route required bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 anchors recognition in self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Access to public and commercial premises is protected by Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk). A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Administrative obligations run alongside the judgments. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Same-sex couples married abroad claim visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights equal to heterosexual spouses by presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office, and the National Registry has instructed all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside Colombia.
outOfScopeNotes:
No reviewed source contains a Risaralda-specific legal provision, enforcement decision, police record or documented incident. The department's profile is therefore an application of the national framework and national incident data, which remains an unresolved gap rather than a finding of local safety or local risk.

The 2025 killing figures differ by source and period — 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025 from one outlet, 35 LGBTI murders January to May 2025 from the Attorney General's Office — and the 2023 and 2024 totals likewise vary between 40-plus, 41 and eight between February and April 2024. Which figures Risaralda's departments report is not sourced.

Whether the Ministry of Interior decree and the 2018 executive decree are implemented by the Risaralda governor's office or the Pereira municipal administration is not stated in the inventory. The status of the comprehensive trans law referenced in earlier drafting is also unresolved: the inventory neither confirms nor denies its passage, and no claim about it is carried here.
